content: Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is a form of optic neuropathy characterized by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) that typically presents within the first few years of life. It is not associated with other systemic or ocular abnormalities. Even in high-income countries, PCG can result in significant morbidity. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the effectiveness and safety of various surgical techniques used to treat PCG. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and others, with the last search performed on April 27, 2020. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared different surgical interventions in children under five years of age diagnosed with PCG. A total of 16 trials were included, involving 587 eyes from 446 children. The majority of the trials (69%) were conducted in Egypt and the Middle East, with others in India and the USA. The follow-up periods ranged from six to 80 months. The surgical interventions compared varied across the trials. Three trials, involving 68 children, compared combined trabeculotomy and trabeculectomy (CTT) with conventional trabeculotomy. Meta-analysis of these trials indicated that there may be little to no difference between the two groups in terms of mean IOP reduction (mean difference [MD] 0.27 mmHg, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.74 to 1.29) or surgical success rates (risk ratio [RR] 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.14) at one year postoperatively. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low due to risk of bias and imprecision. Hyphema was the most frequently reported adverse event in both groups, but no meta-analysis was performed due to significant heterogeneity (I² = 83%). Two trials, involving 39 children, compared viscotrabeculotomy with conventional trabeculotomy. Meta-analysis of 42 eyes showed no significant difference between the two groups in mean IOP reduction (MD −1.64, 95% CI −5.94 to 2.66) or surgical success rates (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.78) at six months postoperatively. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to small sample sizes and risk of bias. Hyphema was again the most common adverse event, occurring in 38% of the viscotrabeculotomy group and 28% of the conventional trabeculotomy group, with no significant difference between the groups (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.83). Two trials, involving 95 children, compared microcatheter-assisted 360-degree circumferential trabeculotomy with conventional trabeculotomy. Meta-analysis suggested that the microcatheter group had lower mean IOP at six months (MD −2.44, 95% CI −3.69 to −1.19) and 12 months (MD −1.77, 95% CI −2.92 to −0.63). Surgical success was also more likely in the microcatheter group compared to the conventional trabeculotomy group (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.21 at six months; RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.97 at 12 months). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was rated as moderate due to small sample sizes. Hyphema was more common in the microcatheter group (40%) compared to the conventional trabeculotomy group (17%), with a higher likelihood of occurrence in the microcatheter group (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.25 to 4.04). The certainty of evidence for this outcome was also rated as moderate. The remaining nine trials each compared different surgical techniques, but no two trials evaluated the same pair of interventions. These included comparisons of CTT with CTT plus sclerectomy, various suturing techniques and adjuvants (e.g., mitomycin C, collagen implants), CTT versus Ahmed valve implantation in previously failed surgeries, CTT versus trabeculectomy, trabeculotomy versus goniotomy, and different types of goniotomy. None of the trials reported data on quality of life or economic outcomes. The authors concluded that there is little to no evidence of a difference in outcomes between CTT and conventional trabeculotomy or between viscotrabeculotomy and conventional trabeculotomy. However, 360-degree circumferential trabeculotomy may offer greater surgical success compared to conventional trabeculotomy. Given the rarity of PCG, future research should focus on multicenter, potentially international trials involving parents of affected children and with follow-up periods of at least one year.
